analysis.one_liner: Charges the largest fossil fuel companies $1 trillion for past emissions to fund climate disaster response.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have billed major fossil fuel companies a combined $1 trillion for their 2000–2022 emissions to pay for climate disaster response, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have charged a one-time $1 trillion assessment to fossil fuel companies responsible for more than a billion metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions between 2000 and 2022, with each company's bill scaled to its share of emissions. Companies could pay in nine annual installments, and the money could not be deducted as a business expense. The proceeds would go into a new Polluters Pay Climate Fund for disaster recovery, climate-resilient infrastructure, and community protection, with 40% reserved for low-income and overburdened communities. It also explicitly preserved the right of states and individuals to sue fossil fuel companies over climate damage.
analysis.who_benefits: Communities hit by climate-driven disasters — floods, hurricanes, wildfires, and extreme heat — would get a dedicated funding stream for FEMA response and resilience programs (at least $15 billion a year, including $3 billion for the FEMA community resilience grant program) and $6 billion a year in Clean Air Act climate grants. Low-income communities, communities of color, and Tribal communities would be guaranteed 40% of the investments. State and local governments, and anyone suing over climate damage, would keep full legal rights against fossil fuel companies.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a one-time $1 trillion assessment on fossil fuel extractors and refiners responsible for more than 1 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions from 2000 through 2022, with each company's bill proportional to its emissions above that threshold and an option to pay over nine annual installments.

Directs at least $15 billion a year from the fund to FEMA for climate disaster response and resilience — including at least $3 billion a year for the Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities program — and at least $6 billion a year to Clean Air Act grants for community climate projects.

Requires 40% of the fund's annual spending to benefit environmental justice communities, defined as communities of color, low-income communities, and Tribal and Indigenous communities facing disproportionate climate and pollution harms.
Bars companies from deducting the assessment as a business expense on their federal taxes, so the cost cannot be shifted onto other taxpayers.

Explicitly preserves every existing legal right of states, local governments, Tribal governments, and individuals to sue fossil fuel companies over climate damage or deception, and prevents the fund payments from being used to reduce any court-ordered damages.

analysis.who_pays: Fossil fuel companies — oil and gas producers and refiners, and coal companies — responsible for more than 1 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions between 2000 and 2022 would owe a proportional share of the $1 trillion, payable in as few as nine annual installments. Because the tax is non-deductible and applies to past activity, some of the cost would likely be passed to consumers through fuel prices over the payment period, and companies could be expected to contest the emissions-attribution formula and the retroactive nature of the levy in court.
analysis.who_pays_short: Largest fossil fuel producers and refiners

drawbacks.text: The assessment is retroactive, reaching emissions from 2000 to 2022 — activity that was legal when it happened. The bill states the tax is not a finding of fault, but companies facing a combined $1 trillion levy on past operations would almost certainly challenge it in court, creating years of legal uncertainty before money flows.

Money in the fund is only available through annual appropriations Acts, so despite the dedicated tax, Congress would still have to vote each year to actually release the money for FEMA grants, climate resilience, and environmental justice projects.

Some of the cost would likely reach consumers through higher fuel prices during the up-to-nine-year payment period, and companies could pass the burden along since the tax applies to their past output rather than future behavior.

The emissions formula assigns set carbon dioxide amounts per barrel of oil, ton of coal, and unit of gas, and the bill gives the Treasury Secretary discretion to adjust company shares — both the formulas and the allocation would be contested by the companies being billed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a very large potential benefit — a $1 trillion dedicated fund for a country already spending roughly $150 billion a year on climate disasters, with 40% guaranteed to the hardest-hit communities — weighed against real design risks: a retroactive levy that invites litigation, an appropriations requirement that could stall the money even if the tax is collected, and some pass-through of costs to consumers at the pump. The strongest good-faith objection is the retroactivity; supporters' answer was written into the bill itself — it claims no fault and leaves every existing lawsuit untouched.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in September 2024 and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never held a hearing or voted on it, and the bill died when the two-year Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Chris Van Hollen introduced the Polluters Pay Climate Fund Act of 2024 on September 12, 2024, joined by five other Democratic senators and independent Senator Bernie Sanders.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance, which has jurisdiction over tax legislation.
No further action was ever taken: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor debate, and no roll call appear in the bill's complete action history.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died in committee, as any bill not passed by both chambers does at the end of a Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The fossil fuel companies that would have owed the $1 trillion assessment are better off, and the roughly $150 billion a year cost of climate disasters stays where it was — on taxpayers and the communities hit by floods, fires, and extreme heat.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel companies that paid nothing

for.name: Sen. Chris Van Hollen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gathered six original cosponsors.

for.name: Sens. Elizabeth Warren, Edward Markey, Jeff Merkley, and Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (Chair Ron Wyden)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote appears in the bill's complete action history.

against.name: Fossil fuel industry trade groups
against.what_they_did: Have long lobbied against polluter-pay assessments and climate liability measures in Congress and against state and local climate lawsuits.

sides.party_line_note: All seven original sponsors were Democrats or the independent Senator Sanders; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill never advanced far enough for a vote that would have shown the full partisan split.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and refiners
industries.note: Companies responsible for more than 1 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide from 2000–2022 extraction and refining would owe a proportional share of a $1 trillion assessment, non-deductible and with joint liability across corporate groups. It died, so they paid nothing.
Coal extraction is covered by the same assessment, with a fixed emissions figure per ton mined, so large coal producers would have been billed alongside oil and gas companies.
